locator: ### The bandwidth reality — "Legacy OpenVPN tunnels compound this: the userspace encryption and TCP-over-TCP pathologies can bottleneck a gigabit link to a fraction of its capacity, even when you are not accessing any internal resource."
problem: Overgeneralizes the TCP-over-TCP (TCP meltdown) pathology to OpenVPN in general. OpenVPN's default and recommended transport is UDP, which does not suffer TCP-over-TCP meltdown. The meltdown only occurs when OpenVPN is explicitly configured to tunnel over TCP. Stating it as a general property of 'legacy OpenVPN tunnels' is misleading; most deployments run over UDP and never hit this.
correction: Scope the claim to OpenVPN-over-TCP: 'OpenVPN configured over TCP (rather than its default UDP) additionally suffers TCP-over-TCP meltdown...'. Keep the userspace-encryption overhead point as a general OpenVPN characteristic, but separate it from the TCP-only meltdown.

refutation.reasoning:
The auditor is correct; I could not refute the finding, and independent authoritative sources confirm it. The doc claim (docs/operations/vpn.md, lines 71-73, "The bandwidth reality" section) states that "Legacy OpenVPN tunnels compound this: the userspace encryption and TCP-over-TCP pathologies can bottleneck a gigabit link," presenting TCP-over-TCP meltdown as a general property of OpenVPN. This is misstated.

Independent verification:
1. OpenVPN 2.4 Reference Manual (authoritative upstream, https://openvpn.net/community-resources/reference-manual-for-openvpn-2-4/): the default for --proto is UDP ("The default protocol is udp when --proto is not specified"), and "OpenVPN is designed to operate optimally over UDP, but TCP capability is provided for situations where UDP cannot be used."
2. OpenVPN Access Server FAQ (the auditor's cited source, https://openvpn.net/as-docs/faq-tcp-meltdown.html): "TCP Meltdown occurs when TCP traffic is tunneled over TCP" and the fix is "Use UDP for the tunnel to avoid this issue." The meltdown is specific to TCP-over-TCP; UDP-mode OpenVPN (the default) does not suffer it.

So TCP-over-TCP meltdown only applies when OpenVPN is explicitly configured over TCP — not the default and not the recommended transport. Attributing it to "legacy OpenVPN tunnels" generally overgeneralizes; most deployments run UDP and never hit it. The claim is also internally inconsistent with the same doc elsewhere (lines 130 and 197) which correctly treats TCP as a fallback for restrictive networks, implying UDP is the default.

The userspace-encryption overhead is a legitimate general OpenVPN 2.x characteristic and should be kept, but the TCP-over-TCP meltdown must be scoped to OpenVPN-over-TCP, matching the auditor's proposed fix. Verdict: misstated (medium). survives=false.

locator: ### The offline root CA approach (recommended) — `mitmproxy --set client_certs=/tmp/debug-session.crt --certs /tmp/debug-session.crt --cert-passphrase ""` (lines 214-243)
problem: The mitmproxy invocation and the security premise of this entire section are technically wrong. (1) `--set client_certs=FILE` configures a CLIENT certificate that mitmproxy presents to UPSTREAM servers for mutual-TLS auth -- it has nothing to do with the CA mitmproxy uses to sign generated certs. (2) `--certs [domain=]path` supplies a custom LEAF/server certificate for specific domains, also not a CA, and its PEM must contain the private key + cert (the example passes only `.crt`). (3) The workflow issues an ephemeral LEAF certificate (`openssl x509 -req ... -days 1`, signed by the root, with no CA extensions) and hands it to mitmproxy expecting mitmproxy to mint per-domain certs from it. That is impossible: mitmproxy intercepts arbitrary HTTPS by SIGNING a fresh per-domain cert for each site, which requires a certificate with `CA:TRUE` and `Certificate Sign` key usage plus its private key. A short-lived leaf cert cannot sign anything. (4) Consequently the stated security benefit ('the root key goes back offline immediately after issuance ... no permanently-exposed signing capability on your machine') is unachievable: a MITM proxy must hold a signing-capable CA private key for the entire interception session. `--cert-passphrase` is also not a documented option (it is `cert_passphrase`, used to decrypt the `--certs` leaf key).
correction: mitmproxy uses its CA to generate per-domain certs on the fly. To use your own offline root CA, place a single `mitmproxy-ca.pem` containing the root's private key AND certificate (X509v3 `CA:TRUE`, key usage `Certificate Sign`) into a confdir and run `mitmproxy --set confdir=/path/to/dir`. There is no way to give mitmproxy only an expiring leaf cert and still intercept arbitrary domains. Rewrite the section to drop the `client_certs`/`--certs`/`--cert-passphrase` ephemeral-leaf workflow and the claim that the signing key stays offline -- during an active session mitmproxy necessarily holds a signing-capable CA key. (Per-domain leaf certs via `--certs domain=path.pem` and upstream client auth via `--set client_certs` are separate, unrelated features.)

refutation.reasoning:
I tried to refute the auditor against authoritative mitmproxy docs and could not; every claim is independently confirmed. Section at docs/operations/proxy-and-capture.md:214-243.

(1) client_certs: Official options doc defines it as "Client certificate file or directory" — certs mitmproxy presents to UPSTREAM servers for mutual TLS, NOT the CA used to sign generated certs. Auditor correct.

(2) --certs [domain=]path: Official certificates doc says it "uses the provided certificate for interception of the specified domain instead of generating a certificate signed by its own CA" — a per-domain LEAF/server cert, not a CA. Its PEM should carry the private key; the doc's example passes only /tmp/debug-session.crt (no key). Auditor correct.

(3) Core security premise is impossible. mitmproxy intercepts arbitrary HTTPS by "on-the-fly generation of dummy certificates for each visited website," signed by its CA. A custom CA must be mitmproxy-ca.pem containing the private key AND a cert with "X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical / CA:TRUE" and "X509v3 Key Usage: critical / Certificate Sign". The workflow issues an ephemeral LEAF cert (openssl x509 -req ... -days 1, signed by the root, no CA extensions) — a leaf cert cannot sign per-domain certs. Therefore the claim that "the root key goes back offline immediately after issuance ... no permanently-exposed signing capability on your machine" is unachievable: a signing-capable CA private key must be present for the entire interception session. Auditor correct.

(4) --cert-passphrase: The documented option is cert_passphrase (underscore), set via --set cert_passphrase=..., used to decrypt the private key supplied via --certs. There is no standalone --cert-passphrase flag as written, and it is conflated with the wrong mechanism here. Auditor correct.

Proposed fix is also accurate: use your own offline root by placing mitmproxy-ca.pem (root key+cert, CA:TRUE, Certificate Sign) in a confdir and running mitmproxy --set confdir=/path; there is no way to hand mitmproxy only an expiring leaf and still intercept arbitrary domains. Verdict wrong (high) holds — survives=false.

Sources: https://docs.mitmproxy.org/stable/concepts/certificates/ and https://docs.mitmproxy.org/stable/concepts/options/ (client_certs, certs, cert_passphrase, confdir definitions); corroborated by mitmproxy discourse "How to use own certificates in mitmproxy".

locator: XFS > Weaknesses: "No checksumming (though metadata checksumming was added in recent versions)."
problem: Misstated/outdated. XFS metadata checksumming (the V5 on-disk format using CRC32c) was introduced in xfsprogs 3.2.0 (2013) and has been the mkfs.xfs DEFAULT since xfsprogs 3.2.3 (circa 2016) — roughly a decade ago, not 'recent.' The non-checksummed V4 format is now deprecated and scheduled for removal from upstream in September 2030. Per mkfs.xfs(8): 'By default, mkfs.xfs will enable metadata CRCs' and 'Formatting a filesystem without CRCs selects the V4 format, which is deprecated and will be removed from upstream in September 2030.' Describing XFS as 'No checksumming' with metadata CRCs framed as a recent add-on understates the current reality.
correction: Reword to: 'Metadata checksumming only (CRC32c), which has been the mkfs.xfs default since ~2016; the non-checksummed V4 format is deprecated and slated for removal in 2030. XFS still does not checksum file data (unlike Btrfs/ZFS), so silent data corruption in file contents is not detected.'

refutation.reasoning:
CONFIRMED the auditor is correct (claim does NOT survive). The doc (docs/reference/platform-setup/disk-strategy.md, lines 328-329) says XFS has "No checksumming (though metadata checksumming was added in recent versions)." This is misstated/outdated on current XFS.

Verified against two sources INDEPENDENT of the auditor's cited man7.org page:

1. Arch Linux mkfs.xfs(8) man page (man.archlinux.org) — current upstream man text: "By default, mkfs.xfs will enable metadata CRCs" and "Formatting a filesystem without CRCs selects the V4 format, which is deprecated and will be removed from upstream in September 2030."

2. kernel.org Patchwork — the actual upstream XFS deprecation patch (20200910182706.GD7964@magnolia): "Support for the V4 format will be removed entirely in September 2030" and the kernel config option "will become default N in September 2025."

Both of the auditor's load-bearing facts hold: (a) metadata CRCs (CRC32c, V5 format) are the mkfs.xfs DEFAULT, and per corroborating sources have been since xfsprogs 3.2.3 (released Oct 18, 2016) — ~10 years ago, not "recent"; (b) the non-checksummed V4 format is deprecated and scheduled for upstream removal in September 2030 (config default already flipped to N in Sept 2025).

Why "No checksumming ... added in recent versions" is wrong: it leads with a flat falsehood (XFS V5 checksums metadata by default) and frames a decade-old default as a recent add-on. The one defensible nugget — that XFS checksums metadata only and NOT file data (unlike Btrfs/ZFS), so silent file-content corruption is undetected — is real and important, but the current doc text does not make that distinction; it instead says "No checksumming." The auditor's proposed fix correctly preserves the data-vs-metadata nuance while removing the factual errors. Verdict: misstated (high). survives=false.

locator: Forbidden Signature Database (dbx) section: "the 2022-2023 \"boot hole\" vulnerabilities triggered several waves of revocations"
problem: BootHole (CVE-2020-10713, the GRUB2 buffer-overflow class of bugs) was disclosed in July 2020, not 2022-2023. The original dbx revocation waves tied to BootHole began in 2020. Dating it to "2022-2023" is off by two to three years and misattributes the timeline.
correction: Change to "the 2020 \"BootHole\" vulnerability (CVE-2020-10713) and its follow-on GRUB2 flaws triggered several waves of revocations" (later dbx updates continued through 2021-2023, but BootHole itself is 2020).

refutation.reasoning:
The doc (docs/reference/firmware/secure-boot.md, lines 58-59) dates the "boot hole" vulnerabilities to "2022-2023." This is wrong. I tried to refute the auditor and could not.

Authoritative upstream sources independently confirm the auditor:
- Red Hat (the auditor's source, https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/grub2bootloader): BootHole CVE-2020-10713 public disclosure "July 29, 2020." Red Hat shipped corrected shim packages Aug 1, 2020.
- Ubuntu Wiki / Debian / SUSE: the FIRST UEFI dbx revocation wave tied to BootHole (revoking the 2012 Ubuntu signing key + GRUB2 binaries) was published August 2020 — described as "the first time large-scale key revocation was needed in the UEFI Secure Boot ecosystem."
- The follow-on GRUB2 flaws were disclosed in 2021 (Canonical "GRUB2 Secure Boot Bypass 2021"; Debian "2021-GRUB-UEFI-SecureBoot"). The SBAT mechanism was created in 2021 precisely because the 2020 BootHole dbx update consumed limited dbx storage.
- Corroborating: NSA advisory (Jul 30, 2020), Eclypsium original disclosure (Jul 29, 2020), Qualys, Oracle, Tenable — all 2020.

Refutation attempt: I searched for any "boot hole" vulnerability in the 2022-2023 window that could justify the doc's date. None exists. The named "BootHole" is unambiguously July 2020; its revocation waves are 2020-2021. Later 2022-2023 dbx activity (e.g., BlackLotus-era updates) is a different, separately-named vulnerability class and is not "boot hole," so it cannot salvage the doc's specific phrasing.

Conclusion: the claim is off by two to three years and misattributes the timeline, exactly as the auditor states. The proposed fix (2020 BootHole / CVE-2020-10713 + follow-on GRUB2 flaws, with dbx updates continuing 2021-2023) matches the upstream record. Verdict stands: wrong. survives=false.

locator: Questions to ask, item 5: "What PCRs are the TPM key bound to? `systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=help` shows the current binding."
problem: This command does not show the current PCR binding. --tpm2-pcrs is an input option that SETS the PCRs to bind during enrollment; it takes a list of PCR indexes/names and does not accept a 'help' value. Running it as shown would attempt a (re-)enrollment, not report state. systemd-cryptenroll has no option to display an existing enrollment's PCR binding.
correction: To inspect an existing TPM2 enrollment's bound PCRs, dump the LUKS2 metadata instead, e.g. `sudo cryptsetup luksDump --dump-json-metadata /dev/nvme0n1p3` and read the systemd-tpm2 token's tpm2-pcrs field (plain `cryptsetup luksDump` shows the token type/keyslot). There is no `--tpm2-pcrs=help`.

refutation.reasoning:
Tried to refute the auditor against independent upstream sources and could not. The doc (docs/reference/firmware/tpm.md, lines 298-300) claims `systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=help` "shows the current binding." That is wrong, confirmed by four independent authoritative sources (Arch, Debian testing, and Ubuntu noble systemd-cryptenroll man pages, plus Lennart Poettering's 0pointer.net systemd blog).

1) --tpm2-pcrs= is an enrollment INPUT option, not a reporter: "Configures the TPM2 PCRs ... to bind to when enrollment is requested via --tpm2-device=. Takes a list of PCR entries..." It accepts PCR index/name (optionally :bank and =digest), not "help".

2) systemd-cryptenroll has NO option to display an existing enrollment's PCR binding. The complete option list (Ubuntu noble) has no --list/--dump/--show/--status for enrollments and no --list-devices; only hardware-token enumeration exists via --fido2-device=list / --pkcs11-token-uri=list (not LUKS slot inspection).

3) Run as written, with --tpm2-device=auto present, it attempts a (re-)enrollment write, not a state report; "help" is not a valid PCR entry so it would fail to parse rather than show anything.

4) The auditor's proposed fix is corroborated upstream: the systemd-tpm2 LUKS2 JSON token stores the binding in a tpm2-pcrs field (Poettering 0pointer.net; token JSON contains tpm2-blob, tpm2-pcrs, tpm2-policy-hash). Read it via `cryptsetup luksDump --dump-json-metadata /dev/...` (plain luksDump shows token type/keyslot). 

Auditor VERDICT (wrong, high) is independently confirmed; survives=false. Suggested doc fix: replace the line with a luksDump-based inspection method. Note: while verifying, I also saw the current man pages state --tpm2-pcrs defaults to binding to NO PCRs (empty), not PCR 7 as older docs said — out of scope for this finding but worth a separate look elsewhere in the page.

locator: Lenovo ThinkPad section: "Bootable CD image (.iso): Can be written to a USB drive and booted directly." followed by `sudo dd if=<firmware-update>.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress`
problem: Lenovo's BIOS Update (Bootable CD) ISOs are El Torito CD images. Writing the .iso directly to a USB drive with raw dd does NOT produce a bootable USB on ThinkPads — the machine will not boot from it. The El Torito boot image must be extracted from the ISO first; only the extracted image is dd-able to USB.
correction: Extract the El Torito boot image first, then dd that image (not the .iso) to USB. Example: `geteltorito -o bios.img <firmware-update>.iso` then `sudo dd if=bios.img of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress`. The geteltorito tool (Debian/Fedora: package 'genisoimage' provides it, or the standalone geteltorito.pl script) is the standard, long-documented way to make a bootable USB from a Lenovo BIOS ISO.

refutation.reasoning:
Auditor is CORRECT; I could not refute it. The doc (docs/reference/firmware/firmware-updates.md, lines 154-162) claims a Lenovo ThinkPad BIOS ".iso" "Can be written to a USB drive and booted directly" via `sudo dd if=<firmware-update>.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M`. This does NOT produce a bootable USB on ThinkPads.

Confirmed by four independent authoritative sources, all describing the same procedure: extract the El Torito boot image first, then dd the EXTRACTED image (not the .iso):
1. ThinkWiki "BIOS update without optical disk" (auditor's own source): dd operates on the extracted bios.img, not the raw ISO.
2. ThinkWiki "BIOS Upgrade" (independent second page): "Use 'geteltorito' to extract the update image from ISO... Write the extracted image to a USB Flash drive using dd" -> `geteltorito g6uj14us.iso > biosupdate.img` then `sudo dd if=biosupdate.img of=/dev/<usb> bs=512K`.
3. Gehrcke (gehrcke.de, 2022, with 2025 comment): `geteltorito -o lenovo-bios.img <iso>` then `dd` the .img; confirmed "works still as expected" on a 2025 ThinkPad X1 Gen12 -- refutes any "modern UEFI ThinkPads behave differently / hybrid ISO" rescue.
4. Debian Manpages: geteltorito(1) is shipped by the 'genisoimage' package, validating the proposed-fix packaging claim.

Root cause: Lenovo BIOS ISOs are El Torito CD images using hard-disk/floppy emulation; the bootable payload is an embedded El Torito boot image, not an isohybrid MBR/GPT layout, so raw dd of the .iso to USB is not bootable (loop-mounting the ISO shows no usable boot files). I found ZERO sources supporting the doc's direct-dd-the-iso claim.

The proposed fix is accurate: `geteltorito -o bios.img <firmware-update>.iso` then `sudo dd if=bios.img of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress`. File to correct: /Users/BillWoika/personal/repos/dotfiles/docs/reference/firmware/firmware-updates.md (the "Bootable CD image (.iso): Can be written to a USB drive and booted directly" line and the dd command beneath it).

locator: Why update firmware -> Hardware compatibility: "add support for new specifications (TPM 2.0 on machines that shipped with TPM 1.2, Resizable BAR on older GPUs)."
problem: Presented as a general firmware-update capability without the necessary caveat. A firmware/BIOS update can only change TPM 1.2 to TPM 2.0 on machines with a firmware-based TPM (fTPM/PTT), and only on specific vendor models (notably some Dell and HP systems with vendor-provided field-upgrade tools). A machine with a discrete (physical) TPM 1.2 chip cannot be upgraded to TPM 2.0 by a firmware update — the chip must be physically replaced. As written, a reader with a discrete-TPM machine would be misled.
correction: Qualify the claim: firmware can upgrade TPM 1.2 to 2.0 only on machines with a firmware-based TPM (fTPM/Intel PTT) and only where the vendor ships a field-upgrade tool (e.g., certain Dell/HP models); discrete TPM 1.2 chips cannot be upgraded by firmware and require hardware replacement.

refutation.reasoning:
REFUTED. The doc (docs/reference/firmware/firmware-updates.md, lines 25-26) lists "TPM 2.0 on machines that shipped with TPM 1.2" as a category of what firmware updates can do. The auditor calls this misleading, asserting that a firmware update "can only" upgrade TPM 1.2->2.0 on firmware-based TPM (fTPM/Intel PTT) and that "a machine with a discrete (physical) TPM 1.2 chip cannot be upgraded to TPM 2.0 by a firmware update — the chip must be physically replaced." That central technical claim is FALSE, and the auditor's proposed fix is also wrong.

Evidence from authoritative chip-vendor and OEM sources:

1. Infineon (the TPM chip manufacturer), OPTIGA TPM developer community: discrete OPTIGA chips are field-upgradable from TPM 1.2 to 2.0 by firmware reflash on the SAME physical chip. The SLB 9660 (discrete, commonly soldered to the motherboard) is reflashed in place and afterward reports as SLB 9665; the SLB 9670 (discrete) has a documented 1.2->2.0 firmware-upgrade path. No chip replacement is involved.

2. Dell publishes "Dell TPM 1.2 Firmware Update Utility ... Nuvoton TPM" (driverid yjvfw) — a firmware reflash of a DISCRETE Nuvoton TPM chip. Nuvoton discrete TPM firmware supports 1.2/2.0 dual-mode switching (fw 1.3.2.8+). Dell KB 000132583 confirms the "Dell TPM 2.0 Firmware update utility" for eligible 2015-2018 models.

3. HP's TPM Configuration Utility reflashes the discrete Infineon (IFX SLB 96xx) chip from 1.2 to 2.0 in EliteBook/ProBook/ZBook and Z-series workstations — these have discrete (often soldered) Infineon chips, not fTPM.

So real-world TPM 1.2->2.0 field upgrades (Dell/HP) are predominantly reflashes of DISCRETE Infineon/Nuvoton chips — the exact opposite of the auditor's assertion that only fTPM/PTT can be converted and that discrete chips must be physically replaced. The auditor's proposed fix ("firmware can upgrade ... only on machines with a firmware-based TPM (fTPM/Intel PTT)") is itself factually incorrect.

Additionally, the auditor's OWN cited source (Microsoft Learn tpm-recommendations, ms.date 2025-08-15) does not support the claim. It describes the three TPM implementation types (discrete/integrated/firmware) but says nothing about discrete chips being non-upgradable or requiring physical replacement. The cited authority does not back the auditor.

On the doc's wording: it is a true, appropriately scoped general statement on a reference page listing categories of firmware-update capability. The phrase "on machines that shipped with TPM 1.2" already signals model/vendor specificity (matching the Dell/HP/Lenovo field-upgrade reality the page elsewhere discusses). It is not wrong, outdated, or misleading on current (2026) hardware. The "misstated (low)" verdict does not survive — the auditor is independently shown to be incorrect, not merely unconfirmed.

locator: ASPM table rows: "| L1.1 | L1 sub-state | 32μs | High |" and "| L1.2 | L1 sub-state | 32-64μs | Higher |"

PCIe L1 sub-state exit latency is implementation-dependent and not fixed by the spec. Authoritative descriptions consistently note that L1.2 (which turns off common-mode voltage, requiring common-mode restore plus PLL relock) has a substantially longer exit latency than L1.1, commonly cited in the ~10-100 us range, whereas the page presents L1.1 at a flat 32 us and L1.2 at only 32-64 us. The numbers understate the typical L1.2 penalty and present false precision for values that vary by device.
correction: Soften to ranges and note implementation-dependence, e.g. L1.1 ~ a few us to tens of us, L1.2 ~ tens of us up to ~100 us, with a note that exact values are device-specific (read from LnkCap/L1 PM Substates capability). Keep the relative ordering (L1.2 > L1.1 > L1 > L0s) which the page already gets right.

refutation.reasoning:
I tried to refute the auditor but could not; independent authoritative sources confirm the auditor is right. The doc (docs/reference/firmware/pcie.md, ASPM table lines 160-161) presents L1.1 at a flat "32μs" and L1.2 at "32-64μs". EVIDENCE AGAINST THE DOC:
1. Linux kernel ASPM documentation (wireless.docs.kernel.org, the canonical Linux ASPM explainer — most authoritative for this firmware/dotfiles context) gives NO fixed L1-substate exit latency. L1 latency is the DEVICE-ADVERTISED maximum shown by lspci as "Latency L0s <512ns, L1 <64us" (a claimed max, not a spec constant), and exit-latency timers are described as reprogrammable/device-specific. The kernel uses LTR + LTR_L1.2_THRESHOLD to choose L1.1 vs L1.2; it does not assume fixed exit latencies. No "32μs" appears anywhere.
2. Synopsys and Electronic Design (PHY IP vendors): L1.1 resumption "on the order of 20 µs", L1.2 "on the order of 100 µs" (commonly cited 10-100 µs). L1.2 is longer because it turns off common-mode voltage keepers, requiring common-mode restore plus PLL relock — exactly the mechanism the auditor described.
3. The auditor's OWN cited Synopsys article (synopsys.com .../reduce-power-consumption.html) confirms the qualitative mechanism (L1.1 maintains common-mode voltage; L1.2 turns off all high-speed circuits) but provides NO microsecond figures — so even it does not back the doc's "32μs / 32-64μs".

WHY THE DOC IS WRONG: (a) "32μs" for L1.1 is false precision — order-of-magnitude is ~20 µs and real values are device-advertised, not fixed. (b) "32-64μs" for L1.2 is false precision AND understates the penalty — the widely cited L1.2 figure is ~100 µs (10-100 µs) due to common-mode restore, so a 64μs ceiling is below the typical. The page even contradicts itself: its own lspci guidance reads latency from LnkCap, and its "L1" row says "2-10μs", yet the substate rows hardcode fixed numbers.

The relative ordering (L1.2 > L1.1 > L1 > L0s) is correct, which the auditor acknowledged. Auditor's stated confidence was low, but my independent check raises it: the figures are wrong/misleading on current authoritative sources. Proposed fix (soften to ranges ~20 µs / ~100 µs, note implementation-dependence, read actual values from LnkCap/L1 PM Substates capability) is correct. survives=false.
